subject: Copywriting
title: Simplicity Is Genius
description: A micro-lesson that makes Simplicity Is Genius usable.

hook.text: 'Think small.' 'Got Milk?' 'Just Do It.' The most powerful copy in history fits on a sticky note.

buildup.text: Bernbach cut. Wieden cut. Every legend removed words until only the essential remained. Brevity was the goal.

discovery.text: Hopkins proved simple copy outsells clever copy. Reeves repeated one message endlessly.

twist.text: Simplicity is the hardest thing to write. Blaise Pascal: 'I would have written a shorter letter but I didn't have time.'

climax.text: Every legend agrees: after writing, cut. Then cut again. When you can't remove anything, the copy is done.

punchline.text: Cut until nothing is left to cut. That's great copy.

quiz.question: What did Blaise Pascal say about writing short?
options: He didn't have time to write a shorter letter

details.summary: From Bernbach's 'Think Small' to Wieden's 'Just Do It,' the legends consistently prove that simplicity is the hardest thing to achieve and the most powerful when achieved. Simple does not mean simplistic — it means distilling complex ideas into their purest, most resonant form.
details.whyItMatters: Complexity is easy; simplicity requires ruthless editing and deep understanding. The ability to say more with less is the hallmark of mastery in copywriting and communication.
takeaways: Simplicity requires more skill and effort than complexity
The best campaigns are built on one powerful idea, not many
Every extra word dilutes impact — edit ruthlessly

faq.question: Why is simple copy harder to write than complex copy?
faq.answer: Simple copy requires you to identify the single most important idea and express it perfectly. Complex copy lets you hedge, qualify, and include everything. Simplicity demands choices — what to leave out is harder than what to include. As Pascal wrote, 'I would have written a shorter letter, but...

faq.question: How did the legends achieve simplicity in their work?
faq.answer: Through relentless editing and a willingness to kill good ideas in service of the great one. Ogilvy rewrote headlines dozens of times. Bernbach insisted on one visual, one idea. They understood that every word must earn its place or be cut.
